content: Prunus virginiana, commonly known as chokecherry, bitter-berry, Virginia bird cherry, or western chokecherry, is a species of bird cherry native to North America. Its natural range spans most of Canada (excluding Yukon, Nunavut, and Labrador), the majority of the United States (excluding some southeastern states), and parts of northern Mexico, including Sonora, Chihuahua, and Baja California. Chokecherry typically grows as a suckering shrub or a small tree, reaching heights of up to 30 feet. Its leaves are oval-shaped, measuring 1 to 4 inches in length, with coarsely serrated edges. The plant produces flowers in racemes during late spring, after the leaves have emerged. The fruits, which are technically drupes, are small, measuring about 0.3 to 0.4 inches in diameter. They range in color from bright red to black and have a highly astringent taste, being both sour and bitter. When fully ripe, the fruits darken in color, becoming less astringent and slightly sweeter. The name chokecherry is often confused with chokeberry, but the two belong to different genera. Chokecherries are part of the Prunus genus, while chokeberries belong to the Photinia genus. Chokecherries are rich in antioxidant pigments, particularly anthocyanins, a trait they share with chokeberries, which adds to the confusion between the two. There are three recognized varieties of Prunus virginiana: 1. Prunus virginiana var. virginiana (eastern chokecherry) 2. Prunus virginiana var. demissa (western chokecherry) 3. Prunus virginiana var. melanocarpa Wild chokecherries are sometimes considered pests because they serve as hosts for tent caterpillars, which can damage other fruit plants. However, cultivated varieties, such as the 'Goertz' cultivar, produce non-astringent and more palatable fruits. Research efforts, such as those at the University of Saskatchewan, aim to develop new cultivars to enhance production and processing. Chokecherries are closely related to black cherries (Prunus serotina), but they are distinguishable by their smaller size, smaller leaves, and sometimes red ripe fruit. Chokecherry leaves are finely serrated, dark green on the upper surface, and paler underneath, whereas black cherry leaves have blunt serrations and a smooth, dark green appearance. The name chokecherry has also been used to refer to the related Manchurian cherry or Amur cherry (Prunus maackii). Chokecherries have historically been a vital food source for many Native American tribes in the Northern Rockies, Northern Plains, and boreal forest regions of Canada and the United States. The bark of the chokecherry root was traditionally used by Native Americans to create a rough-textured preparation for treating colds, fevers, and stomach ailments. The inner bark, along with that of red osier dogwood or alder, was also used in smoking mixtures, known as kinnikinnick, to enhance the flavor of bearberry leaves. The fruit of the chokecherry can be processed into jams, jellies, or syrups, but its natural bitterness requires the addition of sugar to make it palatable. However, chokecherry is toxic to certain animals, including horses, moose, cattle, goats, and deer, particularly after the leaves have wilted due to frost or physical damage. Wilting releases cyanide, which makes the plant sweeter but highly poisonous. Consuming 10–20 pounds of foliage can be fatal to horses, with symptoms including labored breathing, agitation, and weakness. Chokecherry leaves are also a food source for the caterpillars of various Lepidoptera species. In 2007, the chokecherry was designated the official fruit of North Dakota, partly because its remains have been discovered at more archaeological sites in the Dakotas than anywhere else. Additionally, chokecherries are used to produce wine in parts of the western United States, particularly in the Dakotas and Utah, as well as in Manitoba, Canada.
